name: Trad (American Trad)

lead: Trad, often marketed as American Trad, is a narrower, more conservative branch of the Ivy and preppy tradition of American campus dressing. Its staples are oxford cloth button-down shirts, khaki chinos, sack-style blazers and sport coats, and penny loafers or brogues.

People adopt it to look neat, classic and cohesive without chasing trends. The Ivy look dates to the 1920s to 1940s on elite campuses and returned in the early 1980s as preppy and in the 2020s as the old money aesthetic.

paras: Followers build a wardrobe around a few repeatable pieces: an OCBD shirt, chinos, a navy blazer or tweed sport coat, loafers, plus items such as argyle socks and repp-stripe ties. Heritage brands such as Brooks Brothers and J. Press are the traditional sources.
No health risks apply. The main considerations are cost of heritage-brand clothing and fit, since the look depends on cut and proportion.

angle.text: Outfits made of fitted, conservative pieces give a neat and put-together look. Followers say a small repeatable wardrobe makes dressing easy.

lead: Trad, or American Trad, is a style of menswear rooted in Ivy League and preparatory-school dress. It is narrower in scope than the intermediate preppy style, and is often marketed under the label American Trad.[1]

It helps with appearance by giving a consistent, tailored-casual wardrobe: oxford cloth button-down shirts, khaki chinos, blazers and sport coats, and loafers. The Ivy style began as a casualisation of formal menswear with sportswear from polo and tennis, and it spread through campuses in the 1920s to 1940s.[1][2]

Its popularity has moved in waves: about 70% of suits sold in 1957 to 1958 were Ivy-style, young men turned to other fashions in the late 1960s, preppy returned in the early 1980s, and the look reappeared in the 2020s as the old money aesthetic.[1]
infobox: Ivy style, preppy, old money aesthetic

paras: Key garments include the oxford cloth button-down shirt, originally sportswear, worn under suits and sport coats; khaki chinos adopted from military surplus brought by G.I. Bill veterans in the late 1940s; sack jackets with a 3-to-2 roll, no front darts and a single rear vent; and penny loafers or brogues. Other staples are sweater vests, argyle socks, and tweed or houndstooth sport coats.[1]

Preppy dress grew from Ivy style, widespread by the late 1950s and sold on campuses by J. Press and Brooks Brothers. It borrowed from polo, sailing and rowing and from British country clothing.[2] Lisa Birnbach's The Official Preppy Handbook (1980) sparked an 1980s revival, and brands such as Ralph Lauren, Lacoste and Izod brought it to the mainstream.[2]
Polo Ralph Lauren, J. Crew and Vineyard Vines kept preppy clothing in circulation in the 1990s and 2000s, and by the 2010s many dressers moved toward a more tailored look closer to the original.[1]
